# Prerequisites and personnel

This section defines the roles required from the participants, and includes authority and access needs to the working environment.

## Personnel

Focusing on the deployment activity alone, we recommend enlisting a project leader and a cloud administration team. A project leader coordinates events, facilitates resources and assigns duties to the Cloud Administration Team.
Members of the Cloud Administration Team carry out functional tasks to install Terraform Enterprise. For cloud administrators, we make assumptions about general knowledge of the following items.

- Cloud architecture and administration
- Administration-level experience with Linux
- Practical knowledge of Docker
- Practical knowledge of Terraform

In addition, we strongly recommend requesting assistance from a security operations team. The emphasis is on integrating formal security controls required for services hosted in your preferred cloud environment.
It is also essential to specify a role for the production services team who take over the deployment when the project goes live.

## Access

- The installation team requires direct access (including administrator) to the following components to install and configure Terraform Enterprise.
  - Compute/storage instances
  - Network objects such as firewall rules, load balancers
  - Certificates: TLS certificate material
  - Identity such as AWS IAM, GCP Cloud Identity, or AAD
  - Secrets management and associated key management services: AWS Secrets Manager, AWS KMS, GCP Secret Manager, GCP Cloud Key Management, Azure KeyVault, VMware vSphere Native Key Provider
- License File: To deploy Terraform Enterprise you must obtain a license from HashiCorp.
- Certificate authority:
  - Terraform Enterprise requires a TLS certificate and private key on each node. This certificate must match the Terraform Enterprise hostname, either using the FQDN or being a wildcard certificate.
  - Sign the certificate with a public or private CA.
  - The key and X.509 TLS certificate must be PEM encoded. Terraform Enterprise validates the certificate to ensure it uses a Subject Alternative Name (SAN) for Domain Names (DN) entries and not just a Common Name (CN) entry.
  - We recommend a publicly signed certificate where your policy allows it, because every client and integration already trusts it. If you use a private CA, build the certificate file as the full chain in the order server certificate, intermediate, root, and confirm the private key is not passphrase-protected.
  - With a private CA, the CA bundle must contain the full chain for the Terraform Enterprise certificate itself, because Terraform Enterprise calls its own hostname, plus the CA chains of every service it connects to over TLS, such as your VCS, Vault, artifact repositories, Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) relay, and IdP. A missing chain typically surfaces later as failed VCS connections, notifications, or email rather than at install time, so assemble the bundle with the owners of those services before deployment.
  - Convert all certificate material to PEM before deployment. Field teams have had to convert CA bundles delivered in PKCS format. HVD Modules and Kubernetes secrets expect base64-encoded PEM (`base64 -w 0` on Linux, `base64` on macOS). Where a single-line string is required, convert newlines to literal `\n` characters rather than pasting a multi-line value.
  - Workstations and CI runners that use `terraform login` or the API must also trust the private CA chain. Plan distribution of the chain to clients alongside the server deployment.
- DNS: Ensure that a DNS record exists for Terraform Enterprise which matches the SAN in the certificate.

## Secrets bootstrapping

We recommend storing every deployment secret in your cloud secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager) or Kubernetes secrets before deployment, and having the deployment code read them through data sources. This keeps secrets out of `terraform.tfvars`, shell history, and VCS, and gives you one audited location for them. The HVD Modules expect this pattern. Prepare the following:

- Terraform Enterprise license
- Encryption password (`TFE_ENCRYPTION_PASSWORD`)
- PostgreSQL and Redis passwords
- Base64-encoded PEM TLS certificate, private key, and CA bundle

<Warning>

Treat the encryption password as "secret zero." Every Terraform Enterprise node must use the same value, and you cannot restore a backup without it. Store it in a protected location that is independent of the Terraform Enterprise deployment and include it in your backup and disaster recovery plans.

</Warning>

Managed database and cache services restrict which characters a password may contain, and an invalid password fails the deployment late in the apply. For example, Amazon RDS passwords must be 8 to 128 characters and exclude `/`, `"`, `@`, and spaces, and Amazon ElastiCache AUTH tokens must be 16 to 128 characters and exclude the same characters. Field teams have also seen `$` in Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server passwords break deployments. Generate passwords from an alphanumeric character set with a few safe symbols, and check the current constraints of your provider's service before you create them.
